tldr: An LLM agent that reads and rewrites its own Python source in runtime memory — monkey patching, not a fixed optimizer — lifting MGSM accuracy to 64.2% (Meta Agent Search 53.4%) and DROP F1 to 80.9 under GPT-3.5.
method: Gödel Agent is a single Python agent whose main function is recursive rather than a fixed loop, so its own code stays rewritable mid-run. Self-awareness comes from runtime memory inspection: it introspects the local and global variables holding its functions and classes. Self-modification comes from monkey patching — new code is written into runtime memory to add, replace or remove logic. Its action set is self_inspect, interact, self_update and continue_improve: an LLM decision function f0 emits an action sequence from the goal prompt g and environment feedback r=U(E,pi), the action function executes it, and continue_improve recurses one level deeper. Formally pi_t+1, I_t+1 = I_t(pi_t, I_t, r_t, g) — the optimizer updates itself, not just the policy, and the whole code base is rewritten after each execution. Auxiliary tools (think-before-acting, error handling, Python/Bash execution, LLM calls) only accelerate convergence.
results: Table 1, GPT-3.5 for all tests: Gödel-base beats Meta Agent Search on all four benchmarks — DROP F1 80.9±0.8 vs 79.4±0.8, MGSM 64.2±3.4 vs 53.4±3.5 (10.8 points, the paper's '11%'), MMLU 70.9±3.1 vs 69.6±3.2, GPQA 34.9±3.3 vs 34.6±3.2. Hand-designed baselines sit far below (CoT: 64.2/28.0/65.4/29.2).
Unconstrained Gödel-free scores 90.5 / 90.6 / 87.9 / 55.7 (DROP / MGSM / MMLU / GPQA), which the authors attribute to the agent spontaneously requesting help from GPT-4o.

Cost: one complete run — 30 recursive self-improvements across all four datasets — costs about $15 versus $300 for Meta Agent Search, because continuous self-optimization converges faster; the main cost driver is the agent's growing historical memory.

Game of 24 case study: after six failed optimization attempts the agent discards its LLM prompting strategy and rewrites itself to use a search algorithm, reaching 100% accuracy; adding code-assisted verification raises performance by over 10% and reattempting with additional data by more than 15%.

Robustness over 100 MGSM trials: 92% show temporary performance drops and 4% terminate unexpectedly (usually after it edits its own recursive-improvement module), but only 14% end worse than the initial policy. Ablating 'thinking' costs 13.4 points and error handling 14.8 (50.8 and 49.4 vs 64.2); code running (-7.1) and LLM calling (-3.8) matter little.
advantages: Removes the hand-designed meta-level that bounds ADAS / Meta Agent Search: because both the policy and the learning algorithm I are updated, the search space includes the optimizer itself, so the agent can replace its reasoning strategy outright — the Game of 24 switch from prompting to search is the concrete evidence.

One implementation transfers across reading comprehension, multilingual math, MMLU and GPQA with only a task-specific environment description and utility function, versus Meta Agent Search's per-task module design.

Cheap and empirically robust: roughly $15 per full evolution against $300 for Meta Agent Search, and in 86% of 100 trials it recovers from its own bad edits, often by reverting to a previously better algorithm.

Makes the Gödel machine measurable at LLM scale: an explicit recursion between policy and self-referential learning algorithm, a runnable Algorithm 1, and what the authors present as the first fully self-referential LLM agent framework, implemented with monkey patching.
limitations: No direct comparison with the most heavily engineered agent systems such as OpenDevin: the agent must construct all task code autonomously, and the authors say it is unrealistic to expect it to beat systems built over months or years — the experiments demonstrate feasibility of recursive self-improvement, not state of the art.

Gains are bounded by the base LLM: on Game of 24 no initial-policy variant let the agent outperform a hand-written Tree of Thought, and the authors doubt it can innovate beyond state-of-the-art algorithms until LLM capability improves.

Not goal-preserving by construction: self-modification caused 4% of trials to terminate irrecoverably by breaking the recursive-improvement module, and the unconstrained runs' large gains came partly from calling stronger models (GPT-4o), i.e. from leaving the intended setup.

The authors flag an unexplored ceiling — as the system grows more complex through self-optimization it may need exponentially more intelligence to understand itself, so a fully self-referential agent may lose that property as it evolves.
fits: Phase 1 (Foundations & Theory): the self-referential ideal the rest of the arc tests empirically. Pairs with Learning to Learn by GD-by-GD (the improver as a learnable object), STOP and ADAS (its fixed-meta-level foils), and above all DGM (stage 7), which keeps the edit-evaluate gate but adds a never-pruned archive.
reading: Section 3 for the formal recursion and Algorithm 1; Sections 4.1-4.2 for the monkey-patching, memory-inspection implementation and auxiliary tools; Section 5.3 with Table 1 for results; Sections 6.2-6.3 for robustness and Game of 24; Appendix D for the cost comparison.
